subject: Critical Thinking
title: Appeal to Nature: Natural Doesn't Mean Good
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Appeal to Nature: Natural Doesn't Mean Good.

hook.text: 'It's natural, so it must be good for you.' Arsenic is natural. So are earthquakes, cancer, and poison ivy.

buildup.text: Appeal to nature: arguing that something is good because it's natural, or bad because it's artificial.

discovery.text: David Hume identified the is-ought problem: you can't derive what SHOULD be from what IS in nature.

twist.text: The $200 billion 'natural products' industry is built on this fallacy.

climax.text: Nature is indifferent to human welfare. Whether something is good requires evidence of outcomes, not origin.

punchline.text: Natural or not, show me the evidence.

quiz.question: Why is the appeal to nature a fallacy?
options: Being natural doesn't determine whether something is good or bad

details.summary: The appeal to nature assumes that what is natural is inherently good and what is artificial is inherently bad. Arsenic is natural; vaccines are artificial. Naturalness has no logical connection to safety or goodness.
details.whyItMatters: The appeal to nature drives resistance to modern medicine, fear of processed foods, and misguided environmental arguments. Nature is indifferent to human wellbeing.
takeaways: Natural does not mean safe, good, or desirable
Artificial does not mean dangerous, bad, or undesirable
Evaluate products and practices on evidence, not origin

faq.question: Why is the appeal to nature so pervasive in marketing?
faq.answer: Humans evolved in natural environments and have a deep-seated positive association with 'natural.' Marketers exploit this instinct by labeling products as natural, organic, or pure, which triggers trust regardless of whether the label means anything.

faq.question: Is the appeal to nature the same as the naturalistic fallacy?
faq.answer: They are related but distinct. The appeal to nature argues that natural equals good. The naturalistic fallacy, identified by G.E. Moore, argues that you cannot derive 'ought' from 'is.' Both involve errors about the relationship between nature and value.
